paragraphs: The paper presents a neural architecture that learns structure within sequences of symbols. Its target is hierarchical and recursive organization: a smaller unit can sit inside a larger unit, and the same kind of organization can occur at several levels. Recognizing this structure requires more than identifying which symbols appear.

The architecture builds compact descriptions by replacing a substring with a single symbol. That replacement can then participate in a higher-level reduction, allowing the system to work through multiple layers of structure. An external stack provides memory alongside the neural network. Together, these components let the architecture learn to parse strings belonging to LR(0) context-free grammars.

Training uses both accepted and rejected examples, and the authors report learning to recognize many different grammars. Only one layer contains adjustable weights, which makes the learned behavior relatively straightforward to interpret. The contribution is a concrete way to combine learned neural processing, symbolic reduction, and explicit memory to discover nested sequence structure.
neurips-1992-a-connectionist-symbol-mani.tldr: A neural architecture uses symbol reduction and stack memory to learn hierarchical structure in LR(0) context-free languages.

paragraphs: The paper models how people recognize words when they appear briefly in a sequence. Its central concern is timing: recognition depends on how processing unfolds across successive inputs. The authors use this perspective to explain repetition priming, where repetition helps recognition, and repetition blindness, where a repeated word can fail to be detected as another occurrence.

The model introduces a representation of written words built using dynamic time warping and multidimensional scaling. These methods provide the basis for representing relationships among word inputs. The representation then feeds a cascade of three processing stages concerned with perception, comparison, and detection, so recognition emerges through successive transformations of the visual signal.

The authors describe how the changing activity in this cascade can account for several temporal effects in word recognition. The approach matters because it places the helpful and disruptive effects of repetition within a shared processing framework. Its stated contribution is an account of these phenomena through interacting recognition processes that evolve over time.
neurips-1992-a-dynamical-model-of-primin.tldr: A staged dynamical model explains how briefly presented word sequences can produce both repetition priming and repetition blindness.

paragraphs: The paper presents a recurrent neural network for controlling saccades, the rapid movements that change eye position. The task is to connect a command expressed at a neural motor map to an unfolding physical movement. This makes the model an account of movement generation over time, including both horizontal and vertical components.

The network receives the location of a stimulation site on the collicular motor map. It produces the eye's position in the orbit as a time course of two angles. Its units have a one-to-one correspondence with neurons in the intermediate superior colliculus, the brainstem, and the oculomotor system, giving the network an explicit relationship to the biological structures involved.

Simulations demonstrate that the model can reproduce many experimental observations. The stated finding supports the usefulness of this network organization as a model of saccade control. Its contribution is to connect an anatomically specified input, corresponding neural processing units, and a complete movement trajectory within a single computational system.
neurips-1992-a-recurrent-neural-network-.tldr: A recurrent network with biologically corresponding units converts collicular stimulation locations into simulated eye-movement trajectories.

paragraphs: The paper examines a challenge for neural models of cognition: how to represent and compare information whose meaning depends on its internal organization. Compositional representations contain parts arranged into a structure. The authors focus on psychological findings showing that these structured representations matter for human thought, particularly when people make comparisons.

Their account centers on structural alignment. In this process, people compare relational representations by bringing their corresponding organization into alignment. The key issue is how elements relate within each representation, so a model of comparison needs a way to operate on those relationships as well as the elements themselves.

The paper describes a series of psychological phenomena supporting this view and uses them to establish a requirement for cognitive models. Structural alignment must be captured whether a model uses explicit symbols or distributed neural representations. The contribution is therefore a psychologically grounded target for model development: an adequate account of analogy must explain how structured relational information participates in comparison.
neurips-1992-analogy-watershed-or-waterl.tldr: Psychological evidence makes structural alignment of relational representations a core requirement for neural and symbolic models of analogy.

paragraphs: Gradient descent requires choosing how far to move when updating parameters. This paper proposes a principled way to compute that step size using information about the shape of the objective function. The aim is to make learning-rate selection computationally practical even for large backpropagation networks trained on large datasets.

The method estimates principal eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives. These quantities describe prominent directions of curvature and how strongly the objective bends along them. The central computational feature is that the estimates can be obtained without explicitly calculating the Hessian itself, avoiding that matrix as an intermediate requirement.

The authors describe the online version as computationally efficient and use the curvature estimates to determine an optimal gradient-descent step size. They also propose other uses of the same estimation technique, including speeding learning and removing unnecessary parameters. The broader contribution is a reusable way to obtain selected second-order information for training decisions without constructing the full second-derivative matrix.
neurips-1992-automatic-learning-rate-max.tldr: Online estimates of dominant Hessian directions guide gradient-descent step sizes without explicitly computing the Hessian.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a visual system can infer the direction of its own movement from optic flow, the pattern of motion across the visual field. Eye movements complicate this task because the observed visual motion also changes when the eyes move. The authors use a neural network designed to detect heading under these conditions.

The network's performance agrees with human psychophysical observations, and its output units resemble the triple-component cells found in area MSTd of monkey visual cortex. These two connections give the model both a behavioral interpretation and a relationship to measured neural response types within a visual brain area.

The new result is that assumptions about the eye movements an observer is likely to make allow the model to generate additional MSTd cell types. Those assumptions therefore affect the neural responses produced by the heading computation. The finding links variation among modeled cell types to the conditions under which self-motion must be estimated, within one computational account.
neurips-1992-computation-of-heading-dire.tldr: A heading-estimation network reproduces additional visual-cortex cell types when it incorporates assumptions about likely eye movements.

paragraphs: Memory-based classifiers depend on a measure of similarity between an input and stored examples. The paper argues that simple distances between pattern vectors can poorly reflect meaningful visual resemblance. More elaborate matching methods can address this mismatch, but the authors identify computational expense and ad hoc design as concerns.

They propose an efficiently computable distance that can be made locally insensitive to a chosen set of input transformations. Local invariance means that small changes of the specified kinds need not make two patterns appear substantially different. This places knowledge about acceptable variation directly into the comparison used for recognition.

The method was tested on large handwritten-character databases from the Post Office and NIST. The selected invariances covered translation, rotation, scaling, shearing, and line thickness. The authors report that it consistently surpassed every other system tested on those same databases. The result supports the importance of a task-appropriate distance: accounting for transformations that preserve character identity can improve recognition while retaining efficient comparison.
neurips-1992-efficient-pattern-recogniti.tldr: An efficient, locally transformation-invariant distance improves handwritten-character recognition by discounting selected identity-preserving changes.

paragraphs: The paper develops a forecaster for daily peaks and lows in electricity demand within a large Midwestern utility's service area. The application also serves as a test of how to reduce input dimensionality and divide neural-network training into simpler pieces. The central challenge is choosing a workable architecture when many possible input variables are available.

The approach uses projection pursuit to express prediction through simpler components. Weighting vectors combine the original variables into reduced inputs, allowing high-dimensional optimization to become the fitting of single-input, single-output subnetworks. The authors introduce feature-selection and dimension-reduction methods based on an index of level-set dispersion, then combine these methods with backfitting to construct a neural version of projection pursuit.

Training used data from 1989 and 1990, followed by testing on 1991 data. Forecasting performance was comparable to the authors' earlier backpropagation networks. The finding shows that their decomposition can preserve useful predictive performance while reorganizing architecture selection and training around smaller fitting problems.
neurips-1992-forecasting-demand-for-elec.tldr: Dimension reduction and projection pursuit simplify electricity-demand forecasting while matching the authors' earlier backpropagation results.

paragraphs: Inverse kinematics asks which robot configuration produces a desired output position or pose. For redundant manipulators, this relationship is nonlinear and ambiguous. The paper separates two sources of ambiguity: distinct branches of solutions across the configuration space, and extra degrees of freedom within a branch. Each requires its own form of regularization.

For certain classes of manipulators, the authors propose learning from input-output examples generated by the forward mapping. These examples help partition the forward mapping's domain into finitely many regions, resolving the global branch problem. Within each region, an appropriate and consistent parameterization of the redundancy addresses the remaining local ambiguity.

This turns one ill-posed inverse problem into a collection of well-posed problems that can be solved independently. Approximate direct inverse functions can then be constructed for the separate regions. The approach matters because it treats branch selection and redundant freedom as distinct structural issues, giving each a specific role in making learned inverse mappings usable.
neurips-1992-global-regularization-of-in.tldr: Partitioning configuration space and consistently parameterizing redundancy converts certain ambiguous inverse-kinematics problems into separately learnable mappings.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a grammar can be expressed using connectionist computational principles. Its answer is a Harmonic Grammar: a system of soft constraints evaluated together, with well-formed linguistic structures corresponding to solutions of an optimization problem. This gives grammatical specification a form suited to parallel constraint processing.

The stated contribution is to show that formal languages can also be specified this way. Harmonic Grammars had already been applied to problems concerning natural languages; here the approach extends to formal-language descriptions usually expressed through sequential rewrite rules. The significance is that grammatical structure can be defined through the combined demands of constraints.

The supplied text also connects this framework to a broader account of symbolic computation. A representation can be viewed as distributed neural activity at one level and as a symbolic structure at another. Filler-role bindings describe how constituents occupy structural positions. Within this perspective, Harmonic Grammars provide a route for connecting structured symbolic descriptions to underlying connectionist computation.
neurips-1992-harmonic-grammars-for-forma.tldr: Harmonic Grammars specify formal languages through parallel soft constraints whose optimization identifies well-formed structures.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for joining simulated neurons to a biological neural network while that network is operating. A digital signal processing board runs the computer-model components in real time. The result is a hybrid circuit in which known computational elements can participate in the activity of living neurons.

The connections use realistic effective synaptic conductances. This feature matters because the biological neuron receiving a modeled synapse integrates its influence appropriately. The computer model therefore contributes through a biologically meaningful form of connection, allowing its effect to become part of the ongoing network dynamics.

The authors demonstrate this capability as an experimental method. Adding fully specified model elements makes it possible to study how those elements change biological network activity. Adjusting the modeled neuron's parameters also provides a way to assess the contribution of individual conductances, both to that neuron's behavior and to the surrounding network. The contribution is controlled intervention through real-time interaction between computation and biology.
neurips-1992-hybrid-circuits-of-interact.tldr: Real-time conductance-based connections let simulated neurons interact with biological networks for controlled studies of neural activity.

paragraphs: The paper studies object recognition through matching observed parts to stored structural models. A model describes both its parts and their relationships, so successful recognition requires a structurally consistent correspondence. The authors restrict their task to a single object's part labels and continuous parameters, leaving the broader grouping and segmentation problem outside this formulation.

The resulting optimization has two coupled sets of unknowns. Binary variables specify which observed part matches which model part, while continuous parameters determine the weights or costs of those assignments. An optimizing neural network seeks a combination of assignments and parameter values that minimizes the total weighted matching cost.

The proposed improvement is to estimate the continuous parameters before solving the individual part assignments. These preliminary estimates supply a better starting point for the coupled optimization. The authors report that this produces better joint solutions for matching and parameters. The contribution is an initialization strategy that makes use of parameter information available before the discrete correspondences have been settled.
neurips-1992-improving-convergence-in-hi.tldr: Estimating continuous parameters before assigning object parts improves solutions in neural structural-matching networks.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes query by committee, a learning method that selects informative queries from a randomly arriving stream of inputs. Its focus is the relationship between the information obtained from those selected queries and the resulting prediction error. This asks how much learning progress can be attributed to the queries the algorithm chooses.

For a committee with two members, the authors establish a conditional guarantee. If its information gain has a positive lower bound, prediction error decreases exponentially as the number of queries grows. The lower-bound condition means that the relevant information gain remains bounded away from zero, providing the continuing informativeness required by the result.

The authors also show that this exponential decrease applies when learning thresholded smooth functions through queries. This supplies a particular setting where the general information-based guarantee holds. The result concerns error relative to the number of queries, making it a statement about the effectiveness of selective querying and the conditions that support rapid improvement.
neurips-1992-information-prediction-and-.tldr: Two-member query by committee achieves exponentially decreasing prediction error when its information gain stays positively bounded.

paragraphs: The paper uses peg insertion to study whether reinforcement learning can acquire useful control under substantial uncertainty and noise. The task demands precise motion: the clearance between peg and hole is less than 0.2 millimeters. The hole is also unchamfered, so its entrance lacks a beveled edge that could help guide the peg.

Position uncertainty makes the task harder still. The abstract describes uncertainty exceeding the clearance by factors of 10 to 50. Thus, the uncertainty in positioning is much larger than the available fit tolerance. This makes the experiment a test of learned control in conditions where the desired final alignment is far more precise than the initial positional knowledge.

The authors apply direct associative reinforcement learning and report a robust reactive strategy that achieves skillful insertions. A reactive strategy responds as the task unfolds, making the learned controller relevant to the uncertain conditions it encounters. The stated result demonstrates the utility of direct reinforcement learning for this demanding physical control problem.
neurips-1992-learning-control-under-extr.tldr: Direct reinforcement learning acquires robust peg-in-hole control despite positional uncertainty far exceeding the insertion clearance.

paragraphs: The paper describes how existing rules can shape a neural network before training begins. Certain forms of rule-based knowledge determine the initial structure of a network built from normalized basis functions. The authors also give the architecture a probabilistic interpretation, connecting the network's organization to a meaningful interpretation of its computations.

Training must account for the knowledge used to construct the network. The authors describe several ways to preserve that rule-based knowledge as learning proceeds. This makes preservation an explicit part of the method: the initial rules influence both the architecture and the constraints on how it is refined.

The approach also includes complexity reduction, seeking fewer rules and fewer conjuncts, the individual conditions joined within a rule. After training, refined rules are extracted and analyzed. The overall contribution is a workflow that moves from rules into a trainable neural representation and back into inspectable rules, while addressing both knowledge preservation and the simplicity of the resulting description.
neurips-1992-network-structuring-and-tra.tldr: Rule knowledge structures a neural network, guides knowledge-preserving training, and is recovered as simplified refined rules.

paragraphs: The paper presents two working analog vision chips that compute properties of pixel groups. The goal is to move visual processing toward object-level descriptions, where a shared electrical value can represent something about an entire collection of image points. Both circuits are built from networks of resistors and switches.

The first chip implements the dynamic wires model. It establishes dedicated communication among pixels sharing a property and uses that organization to compute contour arclength, the distance along a visual boundary. This produces a collective measurement that depends on how pixels form a contour.

The second chip separates the inside of a contour from its surroundings by assigning the two regions different voltages. Small contour gaps are automatically closed, making its figure-ground separation robust in noisy conditions. Together, the circuits demonstrate hardware operations that organize pixels into meaningful groups and encode group properties electrically. Their stated contribution is a practical step toward object-based processing within analog vision circuitry.
neurips-1992-object-based-analog-vlsi-vi.tldr: Two analog vision chips compute contour length and robust figure-ground separation through electrical representations of pixel groups.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a neural model can estimate an optimal value function online for a control problem. A value function summarizes how well a state can perform under subsequent control choices. Learning such a function addresses a central difficulty of control: an action's full consequences extend into the future.

The proposed strategy uses dynamic programming to obtain local corridor solutions. These solutions supply training information in the form of locally optimal control sequences. A neural architecture then uses that information to model the optimal value function, linking local optimization results to an estimate that can be updated during operation.

The supplied discussion emphasizes that a control action's consequences depend on later actions and the resulting state trajectory. Evaluating the immediate step alone therefore cannot capture its complete effect. The contribution is a general estimation strategy that draws training guidance from local dynamic-programming solutions, providing a way to incorporate future-dependent control information into a neural value model.
neurips-1992-on-line-estimation-of-the-o.tldr: Local dynamic-programming solutions provide training data for online neural estimates of an optimal control value function.

paragraphs: The paper presents an implemented neural model of recognizing familiar objects in scenes containing multiple, potentially overlapping objects. It brings together selective attention, perceptual organization, and transformations supporting invariant recognition. The central question is how these processes cooperate to separate objects, choose what to process, and identify what is present.

Spatially organized feature maps feed two main routes: one represents location, and the other processes object shape and attributes. An early attention mechanism favors a contiguous region of the visual field. That location-based selection also controls normalization within the recognition route, linking where the model attends to how it prepares an object for recognition.

Segmentation separates the scene into entities, while an oscillatory binding mechanism allows multiple segmented entities to be represented at once. Connections between the location and recognition routes coordinate the functional subsystems. The authors report overall behavior consistent with several psychophysical findings. The contribution is an integrated computational account in which attention, grouping, and recognition actively support one another.
neurips-1992-perceiving-complex-visual-s.tldr: An oscillator network coordinates attention, segmentation, and normalization to recognize objects within complex visual scenes.

paragraphs: The paper extends hidden Markov modeling from one-dimensional sequences to two-dimensional images. Its planar hidden Markov model describes image statistics, but usefulness depends on an efficient way to align an image with that model. The authors identify sufficient conditions on model parameters that make planar segmentation solvable in polynomial time.

They provide an algorithm that finds an optimal alignment and accommodates elastic image distortions. The same framework can jointly optimize segmentation and recognition. This coupling addresses a weakness of OCR pipelines that commit to segmentation first: a mistaken division of the image can otherwise create recognition errors that later stages cannot repair.

Evaluation on isolated handwritten digits produced 95% overall recognition accuracy. The authors' analysis found that handling elastic distortions substantially improved performance even in this isolated-character setting. They anticipate greater benefits for connected writing recognition or spotting, but present that as an expectation. The demonstrated contribution combines tractable alignment under stated parameter conditions with recognition that accounts for image deformation.
neurips-1992-planar-hidden-markov-modeli.tldr: Planar hidden Markov models jointly align and recognize distorted images, achieving 95% accuracy on isolated handwritten digits.

paragraphs: Optimal Brain Surgeon removes weights from trained neural networks using all second-order derivatives of the error function. These derivatives describe how parameter changes interact in affecting error. The aim is to retain useful behavior in a smaller network, with potential benefits for generalization, storage, hardware requirements, and subsequent training.

The method depends on a recursive calculation of the inverse Hessian using training data and network structure. The authors report that it removes more weights at the same training error than magnitude-based pruning or Optimal Brain Damage, with better test generalization. In their trained XOR cases, only Optimal Brain Surgeon consistently selected the correct weights to delete.

On three MONK's benchmark problems, the reported weight reductions relative to backpropagation with weight decay were 90%, 76%, and 62%. For NETtalk, the authors pruned a network to 1,560 weights and reported better generalization, compared with the cited 18,000-weight network. These findings support using interactions among parameters when deciding which connections a network can lose.
neurips-1992-second-order-derivatives-fo.tldr: Optimal Brain Surgeon uses full second-order error information to prune more weights while improving reported generalization.

paragraphs: The title identifies the paper's subject as silicon auditory processors used as computer peripherals. It places the work at the intersection of auditory processing hardware and computer-connected devices. This is the only substantive description of the research topic available in the supplied evidence, so the paper can be identified by subject but cannot receive a supported technical explanation.

The supplied abstract field contains corrupted affiliation and contact information, including present-address notices. It does not describe a processor, a connection to a computer, an auditory computation, or an experimental evaluation. Those address fragments provide no basis for explaining what the authors built or how the proposed peripheral operated.

Accordingly, no specific method or finding can be attributed to this paper from this record. Explaining its design, performance, or practical significance would require technical content absent from the supplied text. The supported description remains a paper about silicon auditory processors in a computer-peripheral role; its actual contribution is not recoverable from this abstract field.
neurips-1992-silicon-auditory-processors.tldr: The title concerns silicon auditory peripherals, but the supplied abstract contains only corrupted contact information and supports no technical summary.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how recordings from multiple neurons can be related to underlying network or cognitive states. The data come from extracellular measurements in the associative cortex of behaving rhesus monkeys. The authors seek a statistical description that organizes observed firing activity into interpretable patterns across time and behavioral conditions.

They propose a multivariate Poisson hidden Markov model. Its hidden-state structure represents changing underlying states, while its multivariate observations describe the recorded neural activity. The authors apply it to divide firing patterns into temporal segments and to characterize cortical responses to external stimuli, giving the recordings a state-based organization.

Using this approach, they report significant discrimination between two behavioral modes. The modes differ in their firing patterns and in the coherence of activity across recorded units. The result shows that the fitted statistical structure captures behaviorally relevant differences in population activity. The contribution is a method for connecting multineuron recordings, temporal organization, and behavioral distinctions within one modeling framework.
neurips-1992-statistical-modeling-of-cel.tldr: A multivariate Poisson hidden Markov model segments neural firing and distinguishes two behavioral modes in monkeys.

paragraphs: The paper derives a learning algorithm for separating unlabeled data into clusters using linear discriminants. With no supplied class labels, the learning objective must determine what constitutes a useful division. The authors choose an information-theoretic objective centered on what can be learned by observing a discriminator's output.

The discriminators are robust binary decision units implemented with sigmoid nodes. Training maximizes information gained from their outputs, directing learning toward informative distinctions in the data. This choice differs from objectives focused on preserving information about the full input patterns: the quantity being optimized is tied specifically to the binary decisions.

The authors derive a local weight-update rule by applying gradient ascent to this objective. They demonstrate how the resulting learning dynamics behave on simple datasets, relate the method to earlier work, and suggest possible extensions. The contribution combines a stated information objective with a corresponding adaptation rule, making the connection between the desired clustering behavior and the learning mechanism explicit.
neurips-1992-unsupervised-discrimination.tldr: An information-gain objective yields a local learning rule for clustering unlabeled data with sigmoid-based linear discriminators.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a local learning rule that combines Hebbian adaptation with prediction of a reinforcement signal. Hebbian learning links changes in a connection to the activity of the units it joins. Here, those changes are conditional: an incorrect prediction of reinforcement is what permits the Hebbian update to occur.

This condition gives the reinforcement signal a specific role in directing self-organization. Activity-dependent learning is enabled when the reinforcement prediction fails, tying local adaptation to a discrepancy in what the system expected. The proposed biological interpretation treats reinforcement as the arrival of a neuromodulator at its target, connecting the abstract learning condition to a biological signaling framework.

The authors present three examples applying the framework to development of the oculomotor system, which controls eye movements. These examples demonstrate how the same learning rule can be used in that developmental setting. The contribution is a mechanism for making local Hebbian changes depend on reinforcement prediction, together with a biological interpretation and illustrative developmental applications.
neurips-1992-using-aperiodic-reinforceme.tldr: A local learning rule gates Hebbian adaptation on reinforcement prediction errors, with examples from oculomotor development.

paragraphs: The paper investigates analog circuits for computing visual motion in real time, motivated by the difficulty of doing this on a single chip with integrated sensors. Both proposed schemes estimate speed by measuring the timing of an edge moving through an image. Their shared representation uses pulses with variable duration.

Pulse width provides a direct way to express temporal relationships in the circuit. The first design draws inspiration from Reichardt's model of motion processing in the fly. Its response is non-monotonic with velocity, meaning the output does not change in just one direction as speed increases. The authors present measurements from a chip implementing this design.

The second algorithm produces a monotonic velocity response, giving it a different relationship between speed and output. At the time described, this algorithm was being translated into silicon. The contribution therefore includes a demonstrated pulse-based motion chip and a second proposed design, showing how alternative timing computations lead to different speed-response characteristics.
neurips-1992-visual-motion-computation-i.tldr: Two pulse-based analog motion schemes time moving edges, with chip results for one and a monotonic-response design under development.
